results.summary: This design scrolls the text 'ctag' across a 7-segment display using a 4-state machine built from two flip-flops. It is controlled by a clock and reset input, and the outputs directly drive the seven segment lines. The design is intended for the Wokwi simulator, where the clock can be set to a button to step through the states. It is a minimal demonstration of a scrolling marquee on a 7-segment display.

This design implements a two-player scoreboard that displays an 8-bit score as a two-digit hexadecimal value on a 7-segment display. It uses two counters to track the scores, which can be updated and selected for display via input pins. The design is intended for the Wokwi simulator and requires no external hardware. It is a test run from CNS Lab, demonstrating a simple scoreboard application.

This design implements a PS/2 keyboard interface that accepts hexadecimal scan codes via input pins and transmits the corresponding key press and release signals to a computer. It uses a parallel-to-serial converter to send data according to the PS/2 protocol. The design requires a 3.3V to 5V logic level converter for proper operation. The documentation notes that it most likely does not work, indicating a potential limitation.

This design implements a single FFT butterfly unit with 2-bit resolution, processing two complex inputs to produce two complex outputs. It is intended for the Wokwi simulator and requires no external hardware. The design can be tested by changing the input values. It is a low-resolution demonstration of a fundamental DSP operation.

This design is a test run from CNS Lab, labeled as the second design. It takes a clock and reset input and drives a 7-segment display, but the documentation does not specify its exact function beyond applying inputs and observing outputs. It is intended for the Wokwi simulator and requires no external hardware. The lack of detailed documentation makes it difficult to determine its purpose or behavior.

This design implements an LED chaser effect using the LiteX LED core demo, with the duty cycle controlled by input pins. It is written in LiteX/Migen and synthesizes to Verilog, and it does not include a CPU. The design can be tested by connecting LEDs to the outputs or probing the signals with an oscilloscope to observe a moving train of pulses. It serves as a small demonstration of synthesizing Verilog from LiteX.

This design flashes the letters 'H-E-L-L-O' on a 7-segment display by using a configurable clock divider and a character generator ROM. It includes a debug mode that allows direct indexing of the character ROM and sourcing the slow clock from input pins. The design requires no external hardware beyond a 7-segment display. It is notable for its built-in test harness and configurable flashing behavior.

This design implements a counter that increments or decrements based on rotary encoder input and displays the count on a 7-segment display. It includes a test mode that emulates encoder signals using the clock and an inverted clock. The design requires an external rotary encoder for normal operation. It is a straightforward application of a rotary encoder interface with a display.

Whisk is a 16-bit serial RISC CPU that executes instructions from up to 64 kilobytes of external SPI SRAM. It uses a single SPI interface for instruction fetch, loads, and stores, and internally operates in a fully serial manner to match the SPI memory throughput. An optional IO port interface provides up to 16 outputs and 8 inputs using shift registers. The design requires a host board with SPI SRAM and a host interface for loading programs, and it is notable for its compact serial architecture.

This design implements the XorShift32 algorithm to generate a 32-bit random number, which is truncated to 3 bits and displayed on a 7-segment display. It reads a 6-bit seed value from input pins while reset is asserted, and generates a new number every 1000 clock cycles after reset is deasserted. The design requires no external hardware beyond the 7-segment display. It is a compact hardware implementation of a pseudo-random number generator.
